cues.text: Accused of Sorcery

Dunstan was born around 909 near Glastonbury to a family with connections to the West Saxon court, and was educated by Irish monks and visiting scholars at Glastonbury's ancient abbey, already reputed as Britain's oldest Christian foundation.
As a young man he joined the household of his uncle, Archbishop Athelm of Canterbury, and then the royal court of King Athelstan.
There, his evident talent and closeness to the king provoked jealousy, leading rivals to accuse him of practicing sorcery.
The accusation was grave enough to have him driven from court and, according to a later tradition, thrown into a cesspool by offended courtiers on his way out.
From Exile to Abbot

Shaken by the episode, Dunstan took refuge with his kinsman Aelfheah, bishop of Winchester, who urged him toward monastic life; Dunstan resisted marriage in favor of the religious state, was tonsured, and eventually ordained.
He returned to Glastonbury, living for a time as something close to a hermit in a small cell attached to the old church.
There, he learned metalwork, illumination, and music until King Edmund I — Athelstan's successor — recalled him to court.
When Glastonbury's abbacy fell vacant, Edmund appointed Dunstan its abbot around 943.
A Reformer in Exile and in Power
As abbot, Dunstan began restoring monastic discipline that the disruptions of Viking raids had severely weakened in parts of England, but his standing at court fluctuated sharply with each new king.
Under the unpopular King Eadwig, he was driven into exile in Flanders, where he encountered the vigorous continental Benedictine reform movement firsthand.

He would draw on that experience directly once Eadwig's successor, Edgar, recalled him in 957 and named him, within a few years, bishop of Worcester, then of London, and finally, in 960, Archbishop of Canterbury.
Golden Age of a Kingdom
Dunstan's decades at Canterbury, working alongside two former pupils, produced what later English historians would call a golden age of renewal.
Aethelwold became bishop of Winchester, while Oswald became bishop of Worcester.
Dozens of monasteries were restored or newly founded, clergy discipline was enforced, and law and learning reshaped English religious life for a generation.

Dunstan is traditionally credited with shaping the coronation rite used for King Edgar's crowning at Bath in 973, a liturgy whose essential structure has continued, through many revisions, into the English coronation rite still used today.
Legacy

After Edgar's death in 975 Dunstan secured the throne for Edgar's elder son, later venerated as Edward the Martyr, and weathered the anti-monastic backlash that followed Edward's own assassination in 978.
He spent his final years increasingly withdrawn from politics, devoted to teaching and to the care of his own diocese.
On Ascension Day in 988, he preached three times before predicting, and then meeting, his own death two days later, on 19 May.
Acclaimed a saint almost immediately and formally canonized within decades, Dunstan was regarded as one of England's most prominent saints for much of the Middle Ages.
He held that reputation until the murder of Thomas Becket, two centuries later, in the very cathedral Dunstan himself had once governed.
